# The Hexicon Bug Bounty Methodology

One workflow built from the best public methodologies: scope first, a clear goal per session, wide recon, deep understanding, two-eye testing, proven impact and reports triagers love. Every phase has a goal, a concrete output and the tools to get there.

> ⚠️ Authorized testing only: hunt only on programs you joined and only on in-scope assets, following each program’s rules.

Also on the website, in English, Deutsch, Français, العربية and Русский: https://hexicon-murex.vercel.app/#bounty

## Golden rules

- **5-minute rule**: Nothing interesting on a host after 5 minutes? Move to the next host.
- **20-minute rotation**: Every 20 minutes ask "am I making progress?" If not, rotate: endpoint → host → vulnerability class → target.
- **45-minute cap**: Never spend more than 45 minutes on one parameter. Write it down and come back later.
- **Two weeks, one target**: Stay on one program for at least two weeks (~30 hours). Depth finds unique bugs; hopping finds duplicates.
- **Automate lists, keep judgment**: Tools and AI generate candidates fast. Deciding what is real, proving it and standing behind the report is your job.

<a id="00-scope"></a>
### 00 · Scope & rules

**Goal:** Know exactly what you may test, and how.  
**Done when you have:** A scope file and a list of forbidden actions.

1. Read the whole policy: in-scope and out-of-scope assets, banned tests (DoS, social engineering, spam) and known issues.
2. Write the scope into a file and filter every tool’s output against it.
3. Set tools to the allowed request rate and add any required header (for example your researcher ID).
4. Create your own test accounts — never touch real users’ data.

**Built from:** [Bug Bounty Methodology: The Honest 6-Phase Workflow (XHack)](https://xhack.io/blog/bug-bounty-methodology) · [Crafting your bug bounty methodology (Intigriti)](https://www.intigriti.com/researchers/blog/hacking-tools/crafting-your-bug-bounty-methodology-a-complete-guide-for-beginners)

<a id="01-plan"></a>
### 01 · Mindset & session plan

**Goal:** Hunt with a goal instead of wandering.  
**Done when you have:** One sentence: today I target [feature] to achieve [impact].

1. Pick one impact: steal data, change data, take over an account, or run code on the server.
2. Select one or two vulnerability classes that fit your strengths, and test only those.
3. Choose the route: Wide (new program, wildcard scope, new assets) or Deep (main app, logic and access-control bugs).

**Built from:** [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty) · [Crafting your bug bounty methodology (Intigriti)](https://www.intigriti.com/researchers/blog/hacking-tools/crafting-your-bug-bounty-methodology-a-complete-guide-for-beginners) · [zseano's methodology](https://www.bugbountyhunter.com/methodology/zseanos-methodology.pdf)

<a id="02-recon"></a>
### 02 · Recon: map the attack surface

**Goal:** Find the assets others missed.  
**Done when you have:** A hand-reviewed list of live, in-scope hosts and URLs.

1. Passive first: subdomains from certificate logs, passive DNS sources and code search, then merge and deduplicate.
2. Then active: resolve and brute-force names with good wordlists; for wide scopes add ASN, IP ranges and reverse DNS.
3. Probe live hosts on common and unusual ports; record title, status code and technology.
4. Collect old and crawled URLs (web archives plus a crawler), then deduplicate.
5. Check right away for subdomain takeovers and open cloud storage — these are quick wins.
6. Review the list by hand: dev, staging, admin, internal and odd-port hosts go to the top.

**Tools:** [Subfinder](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/subfinder) · [OWASP Amass](https://github.com/owasp-amass/amass) · [dnsx](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/dnsx) · [httpx](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/httpx) · [Naabu](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/naabu) · [gau (getallurls)](https://github.com/lc/gau) · [waymore](https://github.com/xnl-h4ck3r/waymore) · [Katana](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/katana) · [subzy](https://github.com/PentestPad/subzy) · [reconFTW](https://github.com/six2dez/reconftw)

**Built from:** [Bug Bounty Hunting Methodology 2025 (Amr Elsagaei)](https://github.com/amrelsagaei/Bug-Bounty-Hunting-Methodology-2025) · [Bug Bounty Hunting Methodology 2025 (Phirojshah)](https://medium.com/@phirojshah20/bug-bounty-hunting-methodology-2025-797bf8ae4c27) · [Bug Hunting Methodology: A Comprehensive Guide (Phirojshah)](https://medium.com/@phirojshah20/bug-hunting-methodology-a-comprehensive-guide-619978852f89) · [Red Nexus — Web Application & Bug Bounty Methodology](https://rednexus.academy/en/methodology) · [The Bug Hunter's Methodology (TBHM) — Jason Haddix](https://github.com/jhaddix/tbhm) · [Pentest Book (six2dez)](https://pentestbook.six2dez.com/)

<a id="03-map"></a>
### 03 · Mapping: think like the developer

**Goal:** Understand how the app works before you attack it.  
**Done when you have:** Notes on endpoints, roles, the login model and the key business flows.

1. Use the app as a normal user through your proxy and build the site map.
2. Identify how login works (cookies, JWT, OAuth, SAML) and every role and permission.
3. List the business-critical flows: sign-up, password reset, payments, invitations, data export.
4. Read the JavaScript files for hidden routes, parameters and secrets; discover hidden parameters and API routes.
5. Read the product docs and changelog: what should be impossible? New features are the least tested.
6. Write down anything strange: naming changes, different error formats, old API versions that still answer.

**Tools:** [Burp Suite](https://portswigger.net/burp) · [Caido](https://caido.io/) · [jsluice](https://github.com/BishopFox/jsluice) · [Arjun](https://github.com/s0md3v/Arjun) · [Kiterunner](https://github.com/assetnote/kiterunner)

**Built from:** [zseano's methodology](https://www.bugbountyhunter.com/methodology/zseanos-methodology.pdf) · [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty) · [Crafting your bug bounty methodology (Intigriti)](https://www.intigriti.com/researchers/blog/hacking-tools/crafting-your-bug-bounty-methodology-a-complete-guide-for-beginners) · [Red Nexus — Web Application & Bug Bounty Methodology](https://rednexus.academy/en/methodology)

<a id="04-prioritize"></a>
### 04 · Prioritise

**Goal:** Spend your time where bugs are most likely.  
**Done when you have:** A ranked target list with one reason per target.

1. Rank features and hosts by possible impact and by how likely developers cut corners.
2. Favour new features, complex flows (coupons, refunds, roles), legacy API versions and non-production environments.
3. If one feature has strong checks, look for a similar, newer feature that may not.

**Built from:** [Bug Bounty Methodology: The Honest 6-Phase Workflow (XHack)](https://xhack.io/blog/bug-bounty-methodology) · [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty) · [Crafting your bug bounty methodology (Intigriti)](https://www.intigriti.com/researchers/blog/hacking-tools/crafting-your-bug-bounty-methodology-a-complete-guide-for-beginners)

<a id="05-test"></a>
### 05 · Test with two eyes

**Goal:** Turn every idea into a small, repeatable experiment.  
**Done when you have:** Tested hypotheses with results — including the ones that failed.

1. First eye, systematic — test each input by what it does: IDs → IDOR; URLs and webhooks → SSRF; reflected text → XSS; search and filters → SQL/NoSQL injection; uploads → XSS, RCE, path traversal; prices and coupons → logic and race conditions; login, 2FA and reset → auth bypass; profile updates → mass assignment; templates → SSTI.
2. Second eye, anomalies — look for what feels wrong: exposed credentials, forgotten hosts, admin panels, debug pages, unusual errors.
3. Probe in this order: error-based, then time-based, then out-of-band, then boolean differences.
4. Test access control with two accounts and every role, sideways (user A → user B) and upwards (user → admin).
5. Run scanners for known CVEs and exposures, then move on — manual testing finds the unique bugs.
6. Write down every idea that failed, so you never test it twice.

**Tools:** [Nuclei](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei) · [ffuf](https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf) · [Dalfox](https://github.com/hahwul/dalfox) · [sqlmap](https://sqlmap.org/) · [interactsh](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/interactsh) · [Burp Suite](https://portswigger.net/burp)

**Built from:** [Bug Bounty Hunting Methodology 2025 (Amr Elsagaei)](https://github.com/amrelsagaei/Bug-Bounty-Hunting-Methodology-2025) · [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty) · [HowToHunt](https://github.com/KathanP19/HowToHunt) · [Red Nexus — Web Application & Bug Bounty Methodology](https://rednexus.academy/en/methodology) · [OWASP Web Security Testing Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/) · [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security)

<a id="06-prove"></a>
### 06 · Prove & escalate

**Goal:** Show the real, honest impact.  
**Done when you have:** A working proof of concept with the highest impact you can truly show.

1. Ask "what can an attacker actually do?" and chain small findings into real harm: XSS → account takeover, open redirect → OAuth token theft, IDOR → large-scale data exposure.
2. Cut the prerequisites: aim for zero or one click and realistic conditions.
3. A DNS callback alone is not an SSRF report — show what internal access it gives.
4. Stay within the rules: prove impact with your own accounts and minimal data, and never keep other people’s data.

**Built from:** [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty) · [Bug Bounty Hunting Methodology 2025 (Amr Elsagaei)](https://github.com/amrelsagaei/Bug-Bounty-Hunting-Methodology-2025)

<a id="07-validate"></a>
### 07 · Validate

**Goal:** Submit only real, reproducible bugs.  
**Done when you have:** A finding you reproduced yourself from a clean start.

1. Reproduce it from scratch in a fresh browser session.
2. Check that it is in scope, not on the known-issues or excluded list, and has real security impact.
3. Score severity honestly with the CVSS version the platform uses, matching the impact you proved.
4. If any check fails, drop it — invalid reports cost you reputation.

**Built from:** [Bug Bounty Methodology: The Honest 6-Phase Workflow (XHack)](https://xhack.io/blog/bug-bounty-methodology) · [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty)

<a id="08-report"></a>
### 08 · Report

**Goal:** Make the triager’s job easy.  
**Done when you have:** A report someone can confirm in a few minutes.

1. Title: [Bug type] in [endpoint] lets [attacker] [impact].
2. First sentence: what an attacker can do.
3. Exact numbered steps with the raw HTTP requests, plus screenshots or a short video.
4. Impact, who is affected, and a suggested fix. Short and factual.

**Built from:** [Bug Bounty Hunting Methodology 2025 (Amr Elsagaei)](https://github.com/amrelsagaei/Bug-Bounty-Hunting-Methodology-2025) · [Bug Bounty Methodology: The Honest 6-Phase Workflow (XHack)](https://xhack.io/blog/bug-bounty-methodology) · [Bugcrowd University](https://www.bugcrowd.com/hackers/bugcrowd-university/)

<a id="09-learn"></a>
### 09 · Follow through & learn

**Goal:** Make every hunt improve the next one.  
**Done when you have:** Updated notes and a better personal checklist.

1. Answer triage questions quickly and politely.
2. When the fix ships, test it again — an incomplete fix is a new bug.
3. One bug means the same developer probably made more: spend 20 minutes on similar endpoints.
4. Read public write-ups for the target’s technology, add new tricks to your checklist and automate repeated steps.

**Built from:** [bb-methodology skill — Workflow + Mindset (claude-bug-bounty)](https://github.com/shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty) · [Pentester Land — Bug bounty write-ups](https://pentester.land/writeups/) · [Crafting your bug bounty methodology (Intigriti)](https://www.intigriti.com/researchers/blog/hacking-tools/crafting-your-bug-bounty-methodology-a-complete-guide-for-beginners)
